{{Short description|American biologist}}
 
'''Stuart Alan Newman''' (born April 4, 1945 in [[New York City]]) is a [[professor]] of [[Cell (biology)|cell]] and [[molecular biology|molecular]] [[physiology]] at [[New York Medical College]] in [[Valhalla, New York|Valhalla]], [[New York (state)|NY]], United States. His research centers around three program areas: cellular and molecular mechanisms of [[vertebrate]] [[limb development]], [[physics|physical]] mechanisms of [[morphogenesis]], and mechanisms of morphological [[evolution]]. He also writes about social and cultural aspects of biological research and technology.<ref name="Chuong 2009">{{cite journal| author = Chuong C-M | title = Limb pattern, physical mechanisms and morphological evolution – an interview with Stuart A. Newman | journal= The International Journal of Developmental Biology| volume= 53| issue = 5–6 | pages= 663–671 | year = 2009 | doi = 10.1387/ijdb.072553cc| pmid = 19557675 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Education and background==

Stuart Newman graduated from [[Jamaica High School]] in [[Queens, New York]]. He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] from [[Columbia College of Columbia University]] in 1965, and a [[Ph.D.]] in [[chemical physics]] from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1970, where he worked with the physical chemist, [[Stuart A. Rice]]. He was a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of [[Mathematical and theoretical biology|Theoretical Biology]], University of Chicago and the School of Biological Sciences, [[University of Sussex]], UK, and before joining New York Medical College was an instructor in anatomy at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and an assistant professor of [[biology|biological sciences]] at the [[State University of New York at Albany]].

He has been a visiting professor at the [[Pasteur Institute]], [[Paris]], the ''[[Commissariat à l'Energie Atomique]]''-[[Saclay]], the [[Indian Institute of Science]], [[Bangalore]], the [[University of Tokyo|University of Tokyo, Komaba]], and was a [[Fogarty International Center|Fogarty Senior International Fellow]] at [[Monash University]], Australia. He is a member of the External Faculty of the [[Konrad Lorenz Institute for Evolution and Cognition Research]], [[Klosterneuburg]], Austria and from 2015 through 2025 was editor-in-chief of the institute's journal ''[[Biological Theory (journal)|Biological Theory]]''. He is a director of the [[Indigenous Peoples Council on Biocolonialism]], Nixon, NV and was a founding member of the [[Council for Responsible Genetics]], Cambridge, MA, and of the editorial board of the ''[[Journal of Biosciences]]'' (Bangalore).

==Scientific work==

===Developmental biology===
Newman has been a pioneer in physical approaches to biological [[morphogenesis]] and [[Patterns in nature|pattern formation.]] With the theoretical chemist H.L. Frisch, he proposed a mechanism for patterning of the vertebrate limb [[skeleton]] based on the [[self-organization]] of embryonic tissues.<ref name="Newman & Frisch 1979">{{cite journal |vauthors=Newman SA, Frisch HL | title = Dynamics of skeletal pattern formation in developing chick limb | journal = Science | volume = 205 | issue = 4407 | pages = 662–668 | year = 1979 | pmid = 462174 | doi=10.1126/science.462174| bibcode = 1979Sci...205..662N | s2cid = 44653825 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Sridhar |first=Hari |title=Revisiting Newman & Frisch 1979 |work= ReflectionOnPapersPast |date = 2025|url=https://reflectionsonpaperspast.com/2025/07/03/revisiting-newman-frisch-1979/}}</ref><ref name="Zhu 2010">{{cite journal |vauthors=Zhu J, Zhang YT, Alber MS, Newman SA | title = Bare bones pattern formation: a core regulatory network in varying geometries reproduces major features of vertebrate limb development and evolution | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 5 | issue = 5 | pages = e:10892 | year = 2010 | pmid = 20531940 | pmc = 2878345 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0010892| bibcode = 2010PLoSO...510892Z | doi-access = free }}</ref> The Newman-Frisch model is now the generally accepted basis of tetrapod limb development.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Sheth R, Marcon L, Bastida MF, Junco M, Quintana L, Dahn R, Kmita M, Sharpe J, Ros MA | title = Hox genes regulate digit patterning by controlling the wavelength of a Turing-type mechanism | journal = Science | volume = 338 | issue = 6113 | pages = 1476–1480 | year = 2012 | pmid = 23239739 | doi= 10.1126/science.1226804 | pmc=4486416| bibcode = 2012Sci...338.1476S }}</ref> It provided the index application for the multicellular [[problem solving environment]] [[CompuCell3D]], developed by [[James A. Glazier]] and his collaborators.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Chaturvedi | first1 = R. | last2 = Huang | first2 = C. | last3 = Kazmierczak | first3 = B. | last4 = Schneider | first4 = T. | last5 = Izaguirre | first5 = J. A. | last6 = Glimm | first6 = T. | last7 = Hentschel | first7 = H. G. E. | last8 = Glazier | first8 = J. A. | last9 = Newman | first9 = S. A. | last10 = Alber | first10 = M. S. | title = On multiscale approaches to three-dimensional modelling of morphogenesis | journal = Journal of the Royal Society Interface | volume = 2 | issue = 3 | pages = 237–253 | year = 2005 | publisher = The Royal Society | doi = 10.1098/rsif.2005.0033 | pmid = 16849182 | pmc = 1629079 | issn = 1742-5662}}</ref>

He has also characterized a biophysical effect in [[extracellular matrix|extracellular matrices]] populated with cells or nonliving particles, "matrix-driven translocation", that provides a physical model for [[morphogenesis]] of [[mesenchyme|mesenchymal]] tissues.<ref name="Newman 1985">{{cite journal |vauthors=Newman SA, Frenz DA, Tomasek JJ, Rabuzzi DD | title = Matrix-driven translocation of cells and nonliving particles | journal = Science | volume = 228 | issue = 4701 | pages = 885–889 | year = 1985 | pmid = 4001925 | doi=10.1126/science.4001925| bibcode = 1985Sci...228..885N }}</ref> He is co-author, with the physicist Gabor Forgacs, of the textbook ''Biological Physics of the Developing Embryo'' (Cambridge University Press, 2005).

He has proposed a mechanism of [[cell differentiation]] in animals. Based on a detailed consideration of [[Regulation of gene expression|gene regulatory]] components and processes that distinguish this group from all other forms of life, including their nearest [[holozoa]]n relatives, he has suggested that the [[topologically associating domain]]s found in metazoan embryonic cell nuclei have a unique propensity (due to the presence of [[enhancers]] and [[P300-CBP coactivator family|p300-CBP coactivator proteins)]] to amplify and partition into specialized cells inherent physiological and structural functionalities of unicellular ancestors.<ref name=Newman>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/j.jtbi.2019.110031| title = Cell differentiation: what have we learned in 50 years?| year = 2020| last = Newman | first = SA| journal = Journal of Theoretical Biology| volume = 485| article-number = 110031| pmid = 31568790| arxiv = 1907.09551| bibcode = 2020JThBi.48510031N| doi-access = free}}</ref> This model was the first to propose a central role for [[biomolecular condensate|biomolecular condensates]] in the generation of differentiated cells in [[metazoans]].

===Evolutionary biology===

Newman's work in [[evolutionary biology]] includes a theory for the origination of the [[Metazoa|animal phyla]]. This is proposed to have been driven by new [[Soft matter|physical]] morphogenetic and [[Pattern formation|patterning]] effects set into motion when the products of the ancient [[Evo-devo gene toolkit|developmental-genetic toolkit]] genes first came to operate on the multicellular scale in the late [[Precambrian]]-early [[Cambrian]]. The resulting forms were then [[Canalisation (genetics)|"locked in"]] by [[stabilizing selection]].<ref name="Before programs">{{cite journal |vauthors=Newman SA, Forgacs G, Müller GB | title = Before programs: the physical origination of multicellular forms | journal =  The International Journal of Developmental Biology| volume = 50 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 289–299 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16479496 | doi = 10.1387/ijdb.052049sn| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Newman & Bhat 2009">{{cite journal |vauthors=Newman SA, Bhat R | title = Dynamical patterning modules: a 'pattern language' for development and evolution of multicellular form | journal =  The International Journal of Developmental Biology| volume = 53 | issue = 5–6 | pages = 693–705| year = 2009 | pmid = 19378259 | doi = 10.1387/ijdb.072481sn| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Newman 2012">{{cite journal | author = Newman SA | title = Physico-genetic determinants in the evolution of development | journal = Science | volume = 338 | issue = 6104 | pages = 217–219 | year = 2012 | pmid = 23066074 | doi=10.1126/science.1222003| bibcode = 2012Sci...338..217N | s2cid = 206541349 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/895605 }}</ref>

With the evolutionary biologist [[Gerd Müller (theoretical biologist)|Gerd B. Müller]], Newman edited ''[[Origination of Organismal Form]]'' (MIT Press, 2003). This book on [[evolutionary developmental biology]] is a collection of papers by various researchers on generative mechanisms that were plausibly involved in the origination of disparate body forms during the [[Ediacaran]] and [[Cambrian explosion|early Cambrian]] periods. Particular attention is given to [[Epigenetics|epigenetic]] factors, such as physical determinants and environmental parameters, that may have led to the rapid emergence of [[body plan]]s and organ forms during a period when multicellular organisms had relatively [[phenotypic plasticity|plastic]] morphologies.<ref name = "Epigenetic">{{cite journal|vauthors=Newman SA, Müller GB |title=Epigenetic mechanisms of character origination|journal= Journal of Experimental Zoology|volume=288|issue=4|pages=304–317|year=2000|doi=10.1002/1097-010X(20001215)288:4<304::AID-JEZ3>3.0.CO;2-G|pmid=11144279}}</ref>

Newman has advanced a novel scenario for the origin of birds, the [[Origin_of_birds#Thermogenic_muscle_hypothesis|Thermogenic Muscle Hypothesis]]. Characteristic anatomical specializations of birds, e.g., bipedality, the capacity for flight, are proposed to be secondary to the [[hyperplasia]] of thigh and breast skeletal muscles that arose in compensation for the loss of several genes in [[saurian]] ancestors.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Newman SA | title = Thermogenesis, muscle hyperplasia, and the origin of birds | journal = BioEssays | volume = 33 | pages = 653–656 | year = 2011 | pmid = 21695679 | doi = 10.1002/bies.201100061 | issue = 9| s2cid = 42012034 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Newman SA, Mezentseva NV, Badyaev AV | title = Gene loss, thermogenesis, and the origin of birds | journal = Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences| volume = 1289 | pages = 36–47 | year = 2013 | pmid = 23550607 | doi = 10.1111/nyas.12090 | issue = 1| bibcode = 2013NYASA1289...36N | s2cid = 12240405 }}</ref>

===Inherency and agency in the emergence of phenotypic novelty===

Consistent with his exploration of inherent physical mechanisms of morphogenesis and intrinsic cellular sources of multicellular function, Newman is a critic of [[fitness (biology)| reproductive fitness]] as the basis of [[macroevolution|major evolutionary transitions]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Newman SA | title = Inherency of Form and Function in Animal Development and Evolution | journal = Frontiers in Physiology | volume = 10 | pages = 702 | date = 2019 | pmid = 31275153 | pmc = 6593199 | doi = 10.3389/fphys.2019.00702 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He has argued against the [[Function_(biology)#Selected_effect|selected effect]] theory of biological function in favor of a view that features organismal [[agency (philosophy)|agency]] as the means by which novelties are converted into enablements.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Newman SA | title = Inherency and agency in the origin and evolution of biological functions | journal = Biological Journal of the Linnean Society | volume = 139 | issue = 4 | pages = 487–502 | date = August 2022 | doi = 10.1093/biolinnean/blac109 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Newman SA, Benítez M, Bhat R, Glimm T, Kumar KV, Nanjundiah V, Nicholson DJ, Sarkar S | title = Agency in the Evolutionary Transition to Multicellularity | journal = The Quarterly Review of Biology | volume = 100 | issue = 2 | pages = 83–118 | date = June 2025 | doi = 10.1086/735964 }}</ref>

==Activities around biology and society==

Newman has long warned of dangers associated with lax regulations of genetic engineering of microorganisms and the potential of laboratory manipulation to create new bacterial and viral pathogens.<ref>{{cite journal| author = Newman, SA | title = The "Scientific" Selling of rDNA. |year = 1982| journal= Environment: Science and Policy for Sustainable Development | volume = 24 | pages = 21–57 | url = https://doi.org/10.1080/00139157.1982.9929787}}</ref> In May of 2020 he was among the earliest scientists to speak publicly about the possibility that the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] virus [[SARS-CoV-2]] was constructed in a laboratory.<ref>{{cite web |title=Did the COVID-19 pandemic begin in a lab? Part 1 - Stuart Newman (republished) |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEEqBzs4CSI&t=5s |website=youtube.com |publisher= [[Organic Consumers Association]] |language=en |format=video |date=May 7, 2020}} </ref>   

He has also been an outspoken critic of proposed uses of developmental biology to modify [[Human|human species identity]], including [[cloning]] and [[Human genetic engineering|germline]] genetic manipulation.<ref>{{cite journal| author = Newman, Stuart A. | title= Averting the clone age: prospects and perils of human developmental manipulation| year = 2003|journal = Journal of Contemporary Health Law & Policy | volume= 19| issue= 2| pages= 431–463 | pmid= 14748253|url=http://scholarship.law.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1181&context=jchlp|access-date=2015-09-29}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Newman |first=Stuart A. |title=Opposing Human Genetic Engineering |journal=The CRISPR Journal |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=252–256 |date=August 2025 |doi=10.1089/crispr.2025.0043 |pmid=40397087 |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40397087/ |access-date=}}</ref> In 1997, to encourage public discussion of these emerging technologies, he applied for a U.S. [[patent]] on a human-nonhuman [[chimera (genetics)|chimera]], a composite organism (like the [[sheep-goat chimera|"geep"]]) arising from a mixture of embryonic cells of two or more species.<ref>U.S. patent application no.
08/933,564: "Chimeric Embryos and Animals Containing Human Cells."</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://motherjones.com/politics/2004/01/gods-and-monsters |title=Gods and monsters |last=Dowie | first=Mark |work=Mother Jones |date=January–February 2004 |access-date=July 4, 2011}}</ref> Although the patent was ultimately denied,<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/articles/A19781-2005Feb12.html|title=U.S. denies patent for a too-human hybrid  |last=Weiss |first=Rick |access-date=July 4, 2011 |date=February 13, 2005 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref> it raised [[U.S. Constitution|Constitutional]] and [[Moral philosophy|moral]] questions and was the subject of numerous articles in the legal and philosophical literature. Newman's patent application has been credited with inspiring the provision in the [[Leahy–Smith America Invents Act]] of 2011 that "no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism."<ref>{{cite journal| author = Heled, Yaniv | title= On patenting human organisms or how the abortion wars feed into the ownership fallacy| year = 2014|journal = Cardozo Law Review| volume= 36| pages= 241–298}}</ref> 

His book, ''Biotech Juggernaut: Hope, Hype, and Hidden Agendas of Entrepreneurial Bioscience'' (Routledge, 2019), written with the historian M.L. Tina Stevens, describes the rise of the field of human-oriented biotechnology and presents the scientific case against engineering human embryos.
